related_questions.question: How can I get my smell back after COVID?

text_blocks.snippet: To help regain your sense of smell after COVID, try olfactory training, which involves smelling familiar scents and focusing on recalling associated memories and feelings. This can stimulate the nerve cells in your nose and potentially accelerate the recovery process. Additionally, there is a medical procedure called stellate ganglion block (SGB) that some patients have found helpful, but it's best to consult with a doctor to discuss if this is an appropriate option for you, according to Yale Medicine.

list.title: What it is:
list.snippet: This involves repeatedly smelling specific scents, such as those from essential oils, and consciously focusing on the associated smells and memories.

list.title: How it works:
list.snippet: The process helps to retrain the olfactory nerve cells, which may have been damaged by the virus, by stimulating them and encouraging regeneration of supporting cells.
Gather four scents, like rose, lemon, eucalyptus, and clove.
Take gentle whiffs of each scent for about 25 seconds.
Concentrate on the smell, trying to recall what it looks and feels like, and any memories associated with it.
Do this daily for best results.

list.title: What it is:
list.snippet: A medical procedure where a local anesthetic is injected near a bundle of nerves in the neck, called the stellate ganglion.

list.title: How it works:
list.snippet: The procedure aims to modulate nerve activity and potentially improve blood flow to the nasal passages, which could help with nerve regeneration.

list.title: Consult a doctor:
list.snippet: SGB is not a guaranteed solution and may not be suitable for everyone. It's important to discuss the procedure with a doctor to assess if it's an appropriate option for you based on your individual circumstances.

related_questions.snippet: Smell retraining therapy is simply a matter of sniffing a wide variety of odor-generating elements. About six to 10 different types of scents will do, such as lemons or oranges, flowery perfumes, peanut butter, eucalyptus, rosemary, cinnamon, pine, peppermint, or cloves.

related_questions.question: Does nasal spray help regain smell?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, certain types of nasal sprays may help with regaining the sense of smell, particularly in cases of smell loss related to inflammation or COVID-19. Specifically, fluticasone nasal spray and triamcinolone paste have shown positive results in improving smell and taste function in some patients, according to research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Additionally, a nasal spray containing an active form of vitamin D is being investigated as a potential treatment for smell loss caused by inflammation, according to a UF Health article.

text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options for anosmia (loss of smell) due to COVID-19 are limited and results can be mixed. One approach is smell retraining, and another involves using a dissolvable sponge saturated with platelet-rich plasma (PRP), according to Jefferson Research. This PRP is thought to regenerate damaged cells in the olfactory epithelium.

list.snippet: This involves repeatedly smelling a set of strong odors (e.g., lemon, eucalyptus, rose, clove) to stimulate the olfactory system.
It's a low-risk, readily accessible option that may help improve smell over time.
This treatment involves using a numbing agent, then inserting a dissolvable sponge soaked in PRP into the nasal passages.
PRP is believed to promote the regeneration of damaged supporting cells and olfactory sensory neurons.
Clinical trials for treating anosmia after viral infections, including COVID-19, are still relatively new.
While some patients have shown improvement with these treatments, others may not experience significant changes, according to Yale Medicine.
